claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1g.

claims.claim: NHD mutant Y38C displays diffuse intracellular accumulation in permeabilized cells.
claims.source: We found that the surface expression pattern in non-permeabilized cells was similar for all cell types, whereas in permeabilized cells, the NHD mutant Y38C displayed diffuse intracellular accumulation, in comparison to WT and R47H which displayed a distinct punctate staining pattern (Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: Significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates are found when expressing full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells.
claims.source: Consistent with these observations, we found significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates by anti-FLAG immunoblotting when expressing the full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells (Figure 2h).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: Both Y38C and R47H variants have some signaling potential but neither sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2.
claims.source: Consistent with our observation of FLAG-TREM2 on the cell surface for all the variant proteins, we found that while both the Y38C and R47H variants have some signaling potential, as assessed by phosphorylated-ERK blotting in RAW264.7 and Cos-7 cells, neither of these variants sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2 (Figure 2i,j).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by phospho-ERK immunoblot data shown in Figure 2i and j.

claims.claim: TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic over neutral lipids.
claims.source: In contrast to highly selective phospholipid binding by other Ig domains (Kobayashi et al., 2007; Miyanishi et al., 2007; Santiago et al., 2007; Simhadri et al., 2012), purified TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic (PA, PG, PI, PS) over more neutral (PC, PE) lipids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b and c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA.
claims.source: Moreover, while TREM2 does share a conserved aspartic acid residue from this motif, which chelates a required Ca2+ ion for the TIM and CD300a proteins, TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike TIM and CD300 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e and f).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claims.claim: TREM2 does not bind apoptotic Jurkat T cells which present PS on their cell surface.
claims.source: This is potentially supported by a recent report that TREM2 binds to isolated PS, but does not bind apoptotic Jurkat T cells, which present PS on their cell surface but may also be deficient in GAGs (Bailey et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2015.

claims.claim: TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE.
claims.source: On that note, while this manuscript was in preparation, it was reported that TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE and that this interaction facilitates uptake of Aβ loaded into lipoparticles by microglia (Yeh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh et al., 2016.

claims.claim: TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE.
claims.source: This report also suggests that TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE, but binding affinities were not quantitated.
claims.evidence: This is based on the report by Yeh et al., 2016.

claims.claim: TREM2 can specifically bind GAGs utilizing the basic patch.
claims.source: Our study demonstrates that TREM2 can specifically bind GAGs, utilizing the basic patch; other TREM-like proteins with the same overall calculated pI, but lacking the basic patch residues, do not bind GAGs.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry experiments comparing TREM2, TREML2, and TREML4.

claims.claim: TREM2 AD risk variants affect binding to GAGs.
claims.source: We also demonstrate that TREM2 AD risk variants affect binding to GAGs.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry experiments with TREM2 variants.

claims.claim: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-AAD staining.
claims.source: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD) staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry viability analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2f.

claims.claim: The T96 residue is less conserved in the TREM family but is highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
claims.source: The T66 residue is less conserved in the TREM family, but is highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines.
claims.source: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines from bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and dendritic cells (BMDDCs) in response to FcR (Hamerman et al., 2006) and Tlr signaling (Turnbull et al., 2006; Ito and Hamerman, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines.
claims.source: Likewise, TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines (Takahashi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: TREM2-expressing macrophages can promote inflammatory disease in the brain and lung.
claims.source: However, TREM2-expressing macrophages can also promote inflammatory disease in the brain (Jay et al., 2015) and lung (Wu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Jay et al., 2015 and Wu et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Several classes of molecules have been proposed as TREM2 ligands, including bacterial carbohydrates, sulfoglycolipids, nucleic acids, phospholipids, and proteins.
claims.source: The identity of a physiologic TREM2 ligand (TREM2-L) remains uncertain, although several classes of molecules have been proposed, including bacterial carbohydrates (Daws et al., 2003; Quan et al., 2008), sulfoglycolipids (Phongsisay et al., 2015), nucleic acids (Kawabori et al., 2015), phospholipids (Cannon et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015) and proteins (Stefano et al., 2009; Takegahara et al., 2006; Yoon et al., 2012; Atagi et al., 2015; Bailey et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Cells that express a TREM2-L include astrocytes, DCs, BMDMs, neurons, and apoptotic cells.
claims.source: Additionally, previous studies have identified cells that express a TREM2-L, including astrocytes (Daws et al., 2003), DCs (Ito and Hamerman, 2012), BMDMs (Hamerman et al., 2006), neurons and apoptotic cells (Hsieh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are most significantly dysregulated in late-onset AD.
claims.source: A recent study of more than 1,600 late-onset AD (LOAD) and cognitively normal brains revealed that microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are those most significantly dysregulated in LOAD (Zhang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The TREM2 R47H mutation has been identified in patients with frontal temporal dementia, Parkinson's disease, and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
claims.source: This mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau levels, a well-established risk factor for AD (Cruchaga et al., 2013), and subsequent studies have identified this mutation in patients who have frontal temporal dementia (FTD), Parkinson's disease (PD) (Rayaprolu et al., 2013), and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Cady et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Homozygous TREM2 mutations including early-stop codons, splice site mutations, coding stalk mutations D134G and K186N, and coding ectodomain mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G cause NHD or a frontotemporal dementia variant.
claims.source: Homozygous mutations including early-stop codons (Paloneva et al., 2003; Soragna et al., 2003), splice site mutations (Numasawa et al., 2011; Chouery et al., 2008), the coding stalk mutations D134G and K186N (Paloneva et al., 2002), and the coding ectodomain mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G (Guerreiro et al., 2013a, 2013c; Le Ber et al., 2014) cause either NHD, characterized by early-onset dementia, demyelination, and bone cyst lipoma (Paloneva et al., 2002; Colonna, 2003), or a frontotemporal dementia variant with severe loss of brain matter but lacking the bone manifestations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The coding mutation R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies.
claims.source: In addition to R47H, the coding mutation R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies (Jin et al., 2014; Ridge et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2014 and Ridge et al., 2016.

claims.claim: N68K and D87N have been identified in AD patients, but their risk remains uncertain due to rarity.
claims.source: N68K and D87N have also been identified in AD patients, but because these mutations are very rare, their risk remains uncertain (Guerreiro et al., 2013b; Jonsson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Guerreiro et al., 2013b and Jonsson et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The mutation T96K has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is too rare to allow verification.
claims.source: In addition, the mutation T96K has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is also too rare to allow verification of this observation (Jin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Diffuse Aβ structures are more neurotoxic than dense Aβ plaques.
claims.source: This impacts the density of Aβ plaques and promotes diffuse Aβ structures, which in turn are more neurotoxic, and contributes to the accumulation of classic AD pathology (Wang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016 and Yuan et al., 2016.

results.result: The crystal structure of the human TREM2 ectodomain was determined at 3.1 Å resolution, revealing a V-type Ig domain with nine β-strands, two disulfide bonds (C36-C110 and C51-C60), and a single N-acetylglucosamine glycan at N79. The asymmetric unit contains two similar monomers (Cα RMSD 0.65 Å) that likely do not form a physiological dimer.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13, C14, C58, C59, and C60 are well-supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 1. The resolution determination is justified by systematic analysis (Table 1), and structural features are directly observed in electron density maps. The structural characterization is comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: Nasu-Hakola disease (NHD) mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G are buried within the TREM2 protein core and are predicted to disrupt protein folding through mechanisms including aberrant disulfide formation (Y38C), steric disruption of packing (T66M), and destabilization of the hydrophobic core (V126G). Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15, C16, C17, and C18 are supported by structural analysis (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and solvent accessibility calculations (Figure 1c). The mechanistic predictions are reasonable inferences based on structural data, though they remain predictions. Sequence conservation analysis (Figure 5c) supports the functional importance of these residues.

results.result: Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk variants R47H, R62H, and T96K are located on the TREM2 protein surface. R47 lies parallel to the surface engaging T66, while T96 points away from the surface engaging Q33.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C61, and C63 are directly supported by structural analysis and solvent accessibility calculations shown in Figure 1. The surface exposure of AD variants contrasts with buried NHD mutations, providing a structural basis for distinct disease mechanisms. Structural details are clearly visible in electron density maps.

results.result: NHD mutations impact TREM2 protein stability and folding. While AD risk variants elute as monomers in SEC like WT TREM2, NHD mutants (Y38C, T66M, V126G) elute earlier consistent with aggregation and form covalent dimers/trimers under non-reducing conditions. Flow cytometry shows decreased anti-TREM2 antibody staining for NHD mutants but normal anti-FLAG staining, indicating surface expression of misfolded protein. NHD mutants show diffuse intracellular accumulation and SDS-resistant aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C19-C24, C64, and C65 are well-supported by multiple complementary techniques: SEC (Figure 2a-b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), SDS-PAGE (Figure 2c), flow cytometry (Figure 2d-e), confocal microscopy (Figure 2g), and immunoblotting (Figure 2h). The use of both conformational (anti-TREM2) and non-conformational (anti-FLAG) antibodies provides strong evidence for surface expression of misfolded NHD mutants.

results.result: AD risk variants induce subtle changes in TREM2 structure and stability. R47H shows a statistically significant altered CD spectrum compared to WT, while R62H and T96K do not. All AD variants show slightly lower thermal stability by DSF and chemical denaturation, with T96K showing the most pronounced decrease. All variants show reversible thermal denaturation that is ablated by DTT.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 are supported by CD spectroscopy (Figure 3a-b), DSF (Figure 3c), thermal denaturation (Figure 3d), and chemical denaturation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) experiments. The subtle conformational change in R47H is statistically significant and reproducible across multiple protein preparations. The reversibility experiments with DTT confirm the importance of disulfide bonds for stability.

results.result: TREM2 binds phospholipids with broad discrimination for anionic over neutral lipids, but no differences were observed between WT and AD variant TREM2 ectodomains in direct phospholipid binding assays. TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike other phospholipid-binding Ig domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C34, C67, and C68 are supported by ELISA and liposome sedimentation data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The lack of differences between WT and AD variants in direct lipid binding is clearly demonstrated, though this contrasts with cellular signaling assays from prior work (C32). The EDTA insensitivity distinguishes TREM2 from TIM and CD300 proteins.

results.result: AD risk variants impact TREM2 binding to a cell-surface ligand (TREM2-L). TREM2 tetramers bind to multiple cell lines, and this binding is dramatically reduced by PMA/ionomycin treatment and is sensitive to proteinase treatment, indicating a protein component. The ligand is GAG-dependent, specifically heparan sulfate. R47H shows markedly diminished binding, T96K shows significantly increased binding, and R62H shows intermediate reduction in binding to TREM2-L.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C35-C45 are well-supported by extensive flow cytometry experiments using TREM2 tetramers and monomeric proteins (Figure 4). Multiple complementary approaches (tetramer staining, anti-6His detection, competition assays) consistently show differential binding of variants. The proteinase and heparinase sensitivity experiments (Figure 4d-g) provide strong evidence for the composition of TREM2-L. Cell viability controls (C74) validate the experimental approach.

results.result: TREM2 possesses a large basic surface patch that is not present on other TREM family receptors and is highly conserved within TREM2 but not the rest of the TREM family. This basic patch represents a functional interface for cell-surface ligand binding, as demonstrated by selective binding of TREM2 (but not TREML2 or TREML4) tetramers to cells, and by reduced binding of R76D and R77D mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by electrostatic surface analysis (Figure 5a-f), sequence alignment (Figure 5c), and functional binding experiments (Figure 4i, Figure 5g). The comparison with other TREM family members provides strong evidence for TREM2 specificity. The mutagenesis of additional basic patch residues (R76D, R77D) validates the functional importance of this surface.

results.result: Both Y38C (NHD) and R47H (AD) variants have some signaling potential but neither sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2, as assessed by phosphorylated-ERK in RAW264.7 and Cos-7 cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by phospho-ERK immunoblot data (Figure 2i-j). The experiments show that while both variants can initiate signaling, sustained signaling at later timepoints is diminished compared to WT. This provides functional evidence for impaired TREM2 function in both disease classes, though through different mechanisms.

results.result: NHD mutations are homozygous and lead to complete loss of TREM2 function, while AD mutations are heterozygous and impair but do not completely abolish function. Heterozygous NHD variants have been reported in rare AD cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by genetic analysis and the observed effects of mutations in this study, combined with literature citations (C53 cites Guerreiro et al., 2013b). The dosage model is consistent with the severity and age of onset differences between NHD and AD. However, this represents an interpretive model rather than direct experimental evidence from this study.

results.result: TREM2 can specifically bind GAGs utilizing the basic patch, and TREM2 AD risk variants affect binding to GAGs. Other TREM-like proteins lacking the basic patch residues do not bind GAGs.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C73 are supported by flow cytometry experiments comparing TREM2, TREML2, and TREML4 (Figure 4i), and by heparinase sensitivity experiments with TREM2 variants (Figure 4). The specificity for TREM2 and the impact of AD variants on GAG binding are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The TREM2 R47H variant is associated with AD risk similar to APOE4, correlates with increased CSF tau levels, and has been identified in patients with FTD, PD, and sporadic ALS.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, and C82 are supported by citations to published genetic studies (Cruchaga et al., 2013; Rayaprolu et al., 2013; Cady et al., 2014). These are well-established findings from prior work that provide important context for the current structural and functional studies.

results.result: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on multiple myeloid cell types and is a type one receptor protein consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, stalk, transmembrane domain that associates with DAP12, and cytoplasmic tail.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 are supported by multiple literature citations and illustrated in Figure 1a. These are well-established characteristics of TREM2 that provide essential background for the study.

results.result: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia, and the absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes apoptosis. Microglia do not engulf Aβ plaques, leading to diffuse Aβ structures that are more neurotoxic.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C55, and C87 are supported by citations to published mouse model studies (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016). These provide important biological context for understanding TREM2 function in AD pathology.

results.result: Various homozygous TREM2 mutations cause NHD or frontotemporal dementia. R62H is associated with increased AD risk in independent studies. N68K and D87N have been identified in AD patients but their risk remains uncertain. T96K has been linked to decreased AD risk but is too rare for verification.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by multiple literature citations documenting the genetic associations of TREM2 variants with neurodegenerative diseases. These provide essential context for the variant selection and interpretation in this study.

results.result: Soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages and can be detected in the CNS. Some AD risk variants, but not NHD mutant proteins, are readily detected in patient CSF.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C56, and C57 are supported by citations to published work (Wu et al., 2015; Piccio et al., 2016). These findings provide important context for understanding potential mechanisms by which TREM2 variants affect disease, though they are not directly tested in this manuscript.

results.result: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing inflammatory cytokine production and participating in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells. However, TREM2-expressing macrophages can also promote inflammatory disease in brain and lung.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by multiple literature citations. These provide important background on the complex and context-dependent roles of TREM2 in immune function.

results.result: Several classes of molecules have been proposed as TREM2 ligands, and various cell types express TREM2-L. Microglia-specific networks including TREM2 are most significantly dysregulated in late-onset AD.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by extensive literature citations. These provide important context for the ligand identification efforts in this study and the relevance of TREM2 to AD pathology.

results.result: TREM2 was shown to signal following stimulation of reporter cells by plated phospholipids, and the R47H mutation resulted in loss of signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015. This prior finding provides important context for interpreting the direct phospholipid binding results in the current study, which show no difference between WT and R47H in cell-free assays.

results.result: TREM2 does not bind apoptotic Jurkat T cells which present PS on their surface. TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE, and AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by citations to published work (Bailey et al., 2015; Yeh et al., 2016). These findings from concurrent studies provide additional context for understanding TREM2 ligand interactions, though binding affinities were not quantitated in the cited ApoE study.

results.result: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability (>99% by 7-AAD staining). The T66 residue is less conserved in the TREM family but highly conserved in TREM2 across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 are supported by flow cytometry viability data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f) and sequence analysis. These are important methodological controls and sequence observations that support the main findings.
